title: Wooden Rails and Horse Power
summary: In England, coal miners laid wooden rails across the fields so horses could pull heavy wagons of coal much more easily. Over the next 200 years the wooden rails became iron, the tracks grew longer, and in 1807 people in Wales paid to ride a horse-drawn railway carriage by the sea. The railway was growing up, one hoofbeat at a time!

sections.heading: Coal at Strelley: The Wollaton Wagonway
paragraphs: Picture the countryside just west of Nottingham, in the English Midlands, in the autumn of 1603. Queen Elizabeth I has died that spring, and King James I has just come to the throne. In the fields near the village of Strelley, men are digging coal from shallow pits. They have a problem. The coal is heavy, the local roads are soft and muddy, and the buyers are miles away. Every cartload costs a fortune in horses, drivers and time.

The man trying to solve that problem was Huntingdon Beaumont. He was born around 1560, the youngest of four sons of Sir Nicholas Beaumont, from a gentry family at Coleorton in Leicestershire, a county with coal mines of its own. Being a youngest son meant he would not inherit the family estate, so he had to make his own fortune, and he chose coal. He leased the coal pits at Strelley and went into partnership with Sir Percival Willoughby, the lord of the manor of Wollaton, who owned coal pits nearby. The two men agreed to work the mines as equal partners.

Between October 1603 and 1604, Beaumont built something new: a track of wooden rails running from the Strelley pits to a place called Wollaton Lane End. It was about 3 kilometres (2 miles) long. Horses pulled wagons loaded with coal along the rails. From the end of the line, most of the coal went by road to Trent Bridge and was then loaded onto barges on the River Trent. The wagonway cost £172, a large sum at the time.

Why was this so important? Because it was out in the open, crossing ordinary countryside, built specially to carry goods for sale. The mine tracks we met in Part 1 were mostly short and underground. The Wollaton Wagonway is often called the first overland wagonway in England, and it is the earliest one for which we have clear written records, such as the partnership agreement dated 1 October 1604.

We should be fair to some rivals, though. Historians have found evidence of other very early lines. Wagonways between Broseley and Jackfield in Shropshire, carrying coal down to the River Severn, were operating from October 1605 and might turn out to be just as old, or even older, than Wollaton. There are hints of a wagonway at Prescot, near Liverpool, possibly from around 1600, and of German miners using tracks at Caldbeck in Cumbria decades earlier. Researchers are still digging through old documents, and the race for 'first' is closer than it once seemed.

Sadly, Huntingdon Beaumont's story did not end happily. He took his wagonway ideas north to the coalfield around Blyth in Northumberland, but those ventures lost a great deal of money, much of it borrowed from friends and family. Some historians blame his reckless management. Others argue that he was working mines that were already nearly worn out, and that he actually kept them going far longer than anyone else could have. Either way, he ended up imprisoned for debt and died in Nottingham Gaol in 1624. The Strelley pits were worked only until about 1620, and the Wollaton Wagonway was probably abandoned after that. But the idea he helped launch would never go away.

sections.heading: Black Gold on the River Tyne
paragraphs: To see wagonways really take off, we need to travel north to the coalfields around Newcastle upon Tyne, in north-east England. This region had enormous amounts of coal, much of it close to the surface, and a river that led straight to the sea. London, the biggest city in Britain, was hungry for fuel. As forests shrank and wood became scarce and expensive, more and more Londoners burned coal in their fireplaces, and most of it came from the north-east by ship. Coal from Newcastle was so famous that people began to say 'carrying coals to Newcastle' to mean doing something completely pointless.

The difficulty was the short trip from the pit to the river. Many collieries (coal mines) were several kilometres inland, up on the hills. The coal had to come down to the River Tyne or the River Wear, where it could be loaded onto boats. Doing that by cart on muddy roads was slow and costly, and every landowner whose fields the carts crossed could demand a payment called a wayleave. Building a wagonway along an agreed route, with proper wayleaves, was the answer.

Beaumont brought wooden wagonways to Northumberland in the early 1600s. Over the following century, they spread across the Tyne and Wear coalfield until there was a whole web of them. The Plessey Waggonway, built around 1700, carried coal to the coast near Blyth. By the 1700s, hundreds of kilometres of wooden track were winding across the north-east countryside.

How was a wagonway built? Workers dug a level path and laid wooden cross-pieces called sleepers across it, a bit like the rungs of a ladder lying flat. On top of the sleepers they pegged long wooden rails, usually of oak or another hard wood. Many wagonways later used a clever trick: a second, thinner wooden rail was fixed on top of the main one. When the top rail wore out under the grinding wheels, workers could replace just that strip instead of the whole rail.

The wagons had wheels with a flange, a raised lip on the inside edge of the wheel, which stopped them slipping sideways off the rails. A typical north-east coal wagon, known as a chaldron wagon, carried a little over two and a half tons of coal. That is the weight of about two family cars, all moved by a single horse.

The builders were clever about slopes. Wherever possible, the line ran gently downhill from the mine to the river. A loaded wagon could then roll most of the way by itself, controlled by a brakesman who pressed a wooden brake against the wheel. The horse's hardest job was pulling the empty wagon back up the hill. Later, on some lines, the horse even rode down in a special cart behind the wagons, saving its strength for the climb home.

At the riverside, the wagons ran out onto tall wooden piers called staithes. Trapdoors in the bottom of the wagons opened, and the coal tumbled down chutes into flat-bottomed boats called keels. Teams of tough boatmen, the keelmen of the Tyne, then took the keels downriver to the big sea-going collier ships waiting near the river mouth, which sailed the coal south to London. It was a whole system, from pit to fireplace, and the wagonway was its backbone.

sections.heading: The Causey Arch: A Bridge Built for Coal
paragraphs: As the wagonways grew, so did their engineering. Railways like flat, gentle routes, but the hills and valleys of County Durham got in the way. One of the most impressive solutions still stands today, in a wooded valley near the town of Stanley.

Around 1720, a powerful group of coal-owning families, including the Bowes, Liddell and Montague families, joined forces. People called them the Grand Allies. Together they built a wagonway, later known as the Tanfield Wagonway, to carry coal from inland collieries to staithes on the River Tyne. Its route had to cross a deep gorge cut by a stream called the Causey Burn.

Their answer was a single, soaring stone arch. It was built by a local stonemason named Ralph Wood in 1725 and 1726, and a sundial nearby is inscribed 'Ra. Wood, mason, 1727'. The arch spans about 31 metres (102 feet) and stands about 24 metres (80 feet) above the stream, as high as an eight-storey building. When it was finished, it was the longest single-span bridge in Britain, a record it held for about 30 years, until a bridge was built at Pontypridd in Wales in 1756. The Grand Allies spent about £12,000 on the bridge and its route, a colossal amount at that time.

Two tracks ran side by side across the top of the bridge. Loaded wagons rumbled toward the Tyne on one, and empty wagons came back on the other. Accounts say that at its busiest, more than 900 horse-drawn wagons crossed it every day. Imagine standing below in the valley, hearing the endless clatter of wooden wheels and the clop of hooves high above your head.

The bridge's busy years did not last long. Tanfield Colliery was destroyed by fire in 1739, and traffic over the arch declined. But the bridge itself survived. Today it is called the Causey Arch, and it is thought to be the oldest surviving single-arch railway bridge in the world. It was restored and strengthened in the 1980s and now carries a footpath. Nearby, the Tanfield Railway still runs heritage trains along part of the old wagonway route, operated by volunteers, and it proudly claims to be one of the oldest railways in the world.

sections.heading: From Wood to Iron
paragraphs: Wooden rails had a weakness: they wore out. Heavy wagons grinding along every day chewed into the timber, and rain and frost made it rot. Rails had to be replaced again and again, which cost money and stopped the coal flowing. Engineers wanted something tougher.

The answer came from the iron industry, and especially from one famous place: Coalbrookdale, in the Severn valley of Shropshire. In 1709 Abraham Darby I had rebuilt a furnace there to make iron using coke, a fuel made from coal, instead of charcoal from wood. That breakthrough meant iron could be made in much larger amounts. The Coalbrookdale Company, run by Quaker families, became one of the leading ironworks in the world. Later it would oversee the building of the famous Iron Bridge across the River Severn, the world's first major cast-iron bridge, which opened in 1781.

In the 1760s, the Coalbrookdale Company began strengthening its wooden wagonway rails with iron, fixing cast-iron plates or bars along the top of them, and from 1767 it was making cast-iron rails. A story often told is that the company had more iron than it could sell at the time and laid it on the tracks as a handy way to store it. Whether or not that was the reason, the results were impressive. Iron rails lasted much longer than wood, and wagons rolled along them more easily.

Cast iron had a problem of its own, though. It is made by pouring melted iron into moulds, and it is very strong when squeezed but brittle, which means it can snap suddenly under a heavy blow or bend. Rails had to be short, often only about a metre long, and they could crack. This brittleness would cause big trouble later, when far heavier steam engines rolled onto the tracks.

Over the next few decades, engineers argued about the best shape for an iron rail. One answer was the plateway. Instead of a rail with a rounded top, a plateway used L-shaped iron plates. The flat part of the L carried the wheel, and the upright part, a raised lip along one side, kept the wheel from sliding off. That meant the wagon wheels could be plain, with no flanges at all. John Curr of Sheffield is often credited with using L-shaped plates in collieries around 1787, though historians argue about the exact date. The canal engineer Benjamin Outram, whose Butterley ironworks made rails, became a great champion of plateways, which were often laid on square stone blocks instead of wooden sleepers. Plateways became especially popular in South Wales and the Forest of Dean.

Plateways had one handy advantage: wagons with plain wheels could, in theory, roll off the track and onto an ordinary road. But they also had a big drawback. The flat plates collected stones, grit and dirt, which slowed wagons down and wore out both wheels and plates.

The other answer was the edge rail. Here the rail was a raised bar, and the wheel had the flange, just like the old wooden wagonways and just like trains today. The engineer William Jessop used iron edge rails and flanged wheels on a line opened in 1789 between Loughborough and Nanpantan in Leicestershire, built as part of a canal scheme. In the end, edge rails won, because dirt fell off them instead of piling up, and they suited faster, heavier vehicles. Almost every railway in the world today uses the edge rail and flanged wheel, a design that grew straight out of wooden wagonways.

sections.heading: The Surrey Iron Railway: A Toll Road Made of Iron
paragraphs: Up until now, wagonways and plateways had mostly belonged to mine owners or ironworks, carrying their own goods for their own business. The next big step was a line that anybody could use.

In 1801, Parliament passed an Act authorising the Surrey Iron Railway, south of London. It was engineered by William Jessop, with George Leather as resident engineer, the person who supervised the work on the ground. A short section near Wandsworth opened in January 1802, and on 26 July 1803 the line opened all the way from Wandsworth, on the River Thames, to Croydon, about 8¼ miles (13 kilometres) to the south, passing through Mitcham. With a branch line to Hackbridge, the system was about 9 miles long.

It was a double-track plateway, with L-shaped cast-iron plates set 4 feet 2 inches apart. The railway company did not own any wagons or horses and did not run any trains. Instead, it worked like a turnpike road: anyone could bring their own horse and wagon, pay a toll, and use the track. It was a public railway in that sense, open to all who paid.

What travelled along it? Mostly heavy, everyday goods: coal brought up the Thames by boat, building materials, lime for the soil, manure for farms, corn and seeds. A single loaded wagon could weigh up to about 3¼ tons, and one horse could pull several wagons at once on the smooth iron track, a load that would have been impossible on the rough roads of the time.

The line was soon extended. The Croydon, Merstham and Godstone Railway, opened in 1805, carried the tracks farther south to the stone and lime quarries at Merstham. But the Surrey Iron Railway was never a great money-maker. In 1809 the Croydon Canal opened, competing for the same traffic. The cast-iron plates were also too weak for heavy steam locomotives, which were then being developed. The Merstham extension closed in 1838, and the Surrey Iron Railway itself closed in 1846.

The Surrey Iron Railway is often called the world's first public railway. That is a fair description of what it was, but it may not have been the very first: the Lake Lock Rail Road near Wakefield in Yorkshire, opened in the late 1790s, also let others use its track for a fee. Today, parts of the Surrey Iron Railway's old route lie under later railways and under Croydon's modern Tramlink, so trams still glide along a path first used by horses more than 200 years ago.

sections.heading: All Aboard the Oystermouth Railway
paragraphs: So far, every track in our story has carried goods: coal, stone, ore, lime and manure. But in a seaside corner of Wales, someone had a bright idea. Why not carry people?

In 1804, Parliament passed an Act allowing a horse-drawn tramroad to be built around the curve of Swansea Bay, between the town of Swansea and the village of Oystermouth, near the headland called the Mumbles. It was called the Oystermouth Railway, and its job was to carry limestone from quarries near Mumbles, along with coal and iron ore, to Swansea's canal and harbour. The line was about 5½ miles (about 9 kilometres) long.

In February 1807, one of the original proprietors, a man named Benjamin French, made the company an offer. He would pay £20 instead of tolls for the right to carry passengers along the line for a whole year, starting on 25 March 1807. The company agreed. From that day, a horse pulled a specially built carriage full of paying passengers along the rails beside the sea. Guinness World Records recognises this as the world's first regular passenger railway service.

Imagine taking that ride. You climb into a wooden carriage at Swansea. A single horse leans into its collar, and you start to roll, smoothly and quietly compared with the bone-shaking coaches on the roads. To one side is the sweep of the bay and the sea; to the other, sand dunes and fields. The pace is gentle, about as fast as a horse can comfortably walk or trot, but for its passengers this was something entirely new: a ride on rails, bought with a ticket. The stop in Swansea, known as The Mount, is sometimes described as the world's first railway station, though at first it was little more than a place to wait.

Riding was not cheap. By 1813 the fare was 2 shillings, which only fairly well-off people could afford regularly. By 1823 it had been cut to 1 shilling. Then, in 1826, a new road was built between Swansea and Mumbles. Horse-drawn buses started using it, and passenger traffic on the railway dwindled, until the passenger service stopped altogether for a time.

But the line refused to die. It was carrying passengers again by the 1860s. In August 1877 steam engines arrived, and for a while horse trains and steam trains shared the same track until the horses were finally retired in the 1890s. In 1898 the line was extended to a new pier at Mumbles, and as the area became a popular holiday resort, its trains grew huge, carrying up to about 1,800 passengers at once. In 1929 it was electrified, with big double-decker electric tramcars.

Later known as the Swansea and Mumbles Railway, the line ran for more than 150 years. Its last train ran in January 1960, and buses took over the route. You can still see pieces of its history today, including parts of its tramcars, at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea. Not bad for a line that began with one horse, one carriage and a £20 deal.

sections.heading: The Limits of Horse Power
paragraphs: Let's look back at how far the railway had come in two centuries. In 1604, a short wooden track carried coal across a few fields near Nottingham. By the early 1800s, Britain had hundreds of kilometres of wagonways, plateways and tramroads. Rails had changed from wood to cast iron. Engineers had argued over plates and edges. Tracks had leaped across valleys on stone arches, opened to anyone who paid a toll, and started carrying paying passengers.

And yet one thing had not changed at all. Almost everything that moved on these tracks was pulled by a horse, or rolled downhill by gravity, or was hauled by a rope. Horses are wonderful animals, but they have limits. A horse needs food, water and rest every day. It needs a stable, a groom to care for it, and a blacksmith for its shoes. It can only work for a certain number of hours before it is exhausted. It walks at a few kilometres an hour and cannot keep up a fast pace for long. Even on the best rails, there is only so much weight one horse can move.

Later in the 1800s, when horse-drawn trams filled city streets, the numbers were written down carefully, and they show just how hard horse power was to scale up. A typical tram horse worked only four or five hours a day and covered about 19 kilometres (12 miles). Many tram companies kept ten or more horses in their stables for every single tramcar, and a hard-working tram horse might last only a few years before it was worn out. The early wagonway owners faced the same arithmetic: double the traffic, and you had to double the horses, the hay, the stables and the stable hands.

Busy railways needed lots of horses, and a lot of money to look after them. And as more coal mines, ironworks and factories opened during the Industrial Revolution, the demand for moving heavy goods kept growing faster and faster.

Meanwhile, in the mines themselves, a new kind of power was already at work. For decades, enormous engines driven by steam had been pumping water out of deep mine shafts, working day and night without ever growing tired. They were huge, heavy and fixed in place, so nobody had yet put one on wheels. But engineers were starting to wonder.
What if something stronger than a horse, something that never got tired, never needed to sleep, and could keep going all day and all night, could pull the wagons?

deepDive: Railway 'firsts' from this period are a minefield, and how you word a claim matters. The Wollaton Wagonway (1603–1604) is often called the first railway in England, but that really means the first overland wagonway with solid documentary proof. Shropshire wagonways at Broseley were running by October 1605, and a 2014 study by historians of early railways was titled, tellingly, 'Wollaton or Broseley? The gap narrows'. There are also earlier hints at Prescot and at Caldbeck. Historians reasonably disagree because the evidence consists of leases, lawsuits and account books, not photographs, and a single newly found document can shift the date. Huntingdon Beaumont's reputation is debated too. One older study blamed his ruin on reckless management, while more recent work argues that he inherited nearly exhausted coal seams and kept them productive for about twenty extra years. The 'first public railway' title is just as slippery. The Surrey Iron Railway (opened 26 July 1803) is often given it, because it was authorised by Parliament as a public toll line open to any user. But the Lake Lock Rail Road in West Yorkshire, opened in the late 1790s, also operated publicly and is sometimes described as the world's oldest public railway. Similarly, the Oystermouth Railway's 1807 service is the first known regular fare-paying passenger service, recognised by Guinness World Records, but earlier lines may occasionally have carried people informally. The technical debate is clearer in hindsight. Cast iron is strong in compression but weak in tension and brittle, so short cast rails cracked under load. Plateways put the guiding flange on the rail, letting plain wheels run, but the flat plate trapped grit and greatly increased rolling resistance. Edge rails shed dirt and allowed a smaller contact patch, so friction was lower. Once rolled wrought-iron rails arrived in 1820, long strong edge rails became practical, and the plateway faded. A simple test settles the 'horse power' question: on a level road a horse might pull around a ton, but on smooth iron rails it could pull several loaded wagons, many times more.
funFact: The Swansea and Mumbles Railway carried passengers with horses, then steam engines, then electric trams, and kept running for more than 150 years before closing in January 1960.
